doc.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Working at inspiration; sound and the alto tradition
summary: He works at inspiration and orchestrates at the computer; Hodges and Benny Carter taught him that sound comes first on the alto.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So you’re easily inspired, aren’t you?

Yeah, I am. I work at it though. I work at inspiration. I think it’s, you know 90% perspiration and a little inspiration. But I mean I do all my writing at the computer, I mean I work at the keyboard, get the ideas and all that, but then I go right to the computer and and orchestrate and I find it great convenience to be able to hear it while I’m writing, orchestrating anyway. I don’t think you can create at the computer but for orchestration it’s great.
Did Johnny Hodges instill in that if you don’t have a sound you don’t have anything?

Oh yeah, but Benny Carter too. You know, that whole early tradition of the alto saxophone. I mean, if you go to the movies and you hear an alto, somebody’s kissing or somebody’s dying. [both laugh] It’s a very romantic or perilous instrument, you know what I mean? But it always signifies something very deep. Especially the alto, you know.
